rows.description: A young professional meets someone through friends or a matchmaking family. Attraction is present but tempered by questions on career, city and readiness, so excitement and caution share the same evening.
They text morning to night, share meals and start planning weekends. Small acts of dependability such as remembering a deadline matter more now than grand gestures.
A disagreement over money, time with parents or work travel reveals different expectations. How each behaves in the first real disagreement says more about the future than the honeymoon months.

rows.subtype: Stage 4: Fear of loss of freedom [Actor]
rows.description: One becomes quieter as talk of living together nears, feeling both love and a sense of a closing door. Ambivalence is normal; hiding it is the risk, and saying it early is the kinder path.

They discuss what commitment means: where to live, family, children, careers and each other's parents. Concrete talk replaces vague reassurance, and disagreement found now is cheaper than after a wedding.

rows.subtype: Stage 6: Choosing each other, with eyes open [Response]
rows.description: The couple commits knowing the other's flaws and trusting their way of resolving trouble. A steady bond built on respect tends to hold better than one built on intensity.
An intern is told by a senior to redo a report with little explanation. She feels criticised, unsure whether she failed or the senior is simply busy, and she is afraid to ask.
The senior takes her silence for lack of interest, and she takes his brisk tone for dislike. New workers often assume feedback is personal, and busy seniors often forget they need to explain.
In a team meeting the senior points out her error in front of others. She feels heat in her face and swallows her reply, then spends the evening rehearsing what she should have said.

Rather than complaining to peers, she requests a short private talk: "I want to do this well. Could you tell me what to improve, and could feedback be given privately when possible?" Calm clarity is professional and often welcomed.
He realises that he had assumed she knew the standard and had been careless with her dignity. A good senior acknowledges the way it was said without dropping the content of the correction.
They agree on a quick weekly check-in and written expectations. She learns that conflict at work can be raised respectfully, and that it grows trust more than swallowing resentment does.

rows.subtype: Stage 1: A hurt that is not spoken [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager feels ignored when her friend sits with others at lunch. She is too proud to ask about it and too hurt to act normal, so she says nothing and turns her face away.
Not replying feels safer than risking a fight or hearing "you are overreacting". Silence gives her a sense of control, and part of her hopes the friend will notice and come to her.

rows.subtype: Stage 3: Confusion for the one ignored [Receiver]
rows.description: The friend cannot tell what she did. Being unanswered feels like exclusion, so she guesses wildly, rereads old chats and grows anxious, which is precisely why silence hurts more than open anger.
Days pass and the silence becomes a message: you should know what you did. The teen enjoys being wanted back yet feels lonelier, and with every day, breaking the silence gets more embarrassing.
The friend sends "I can feel you are upset and I do not know why. I would rather hear it, even if it is bad." An invitation without accusation makes speaking safer than staying quiet.
The teen says "I felt left out at lunch." The reply is usually smaller than the fear, and both learn that saying it early costs less than months of quiet distance.
